chunks: "They're mirror images. An NPN is an N-type emitter, a thin P-type base and an N-type collector, and its main carriers are electrons.
A PNP swaps all the doping types, so the main carriers are holes. In circuit terms everything flips polarity. An NPN turns on when the base is about 0.
7 volts above the emitter, current flows into the collector and base and out of the emitter, and the collector is the positive side, so it's the natural low-side switch with the emitter on ground.
A PNP turns on when the base is about 0.
7 volts below the emitter, current flows into the emitter and out of the base and collector, and the emitter goes to the positive supply, so it's the natural high-side switch.

Holes are about three times less mobile than electrons in silicon, so for the same geometry a PNP has a longer transit time, a lower transition frequency and typically lower gain, and integrated PNPs are particularly weak.
That's why analogue ICs lean on NPN, and why 2N3904 and 2N3906, the complementary pair, are specified similarly but the PNP is a bit slower.
They're used together in complementary stages, for example a push-pull output where the NPN sources current and the PNP sinks it.
The symbol arrow on the emitter points out for NPN and in for PNP."
